meta.title: Who really said "When you arise in the morning, think of what a precious privilege it is to be alive - to breathe, to think, to enjoy, to love"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Not Marcus Aurelius. This morning-gratitude line is an Elbert Hubbard epigram from his magazine The Fra (c. 1914) — it is in no translation of the Meditations.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'When you arise in the morning, think of what a precious privilege it is to be alive - to breathe, to think, to enjoy, to love'?

answer.label: Not Marcus Aurelius — actually Elbert Hubbard
answer.authorDates: 1856–1915 · American writer, publisher & founder of the Roycroft community
answer.sourceLine: This line appears in no translation of Marcus Aurelius’s Meditations. It is an epigram by the American writer Elbert Hubbard, printed in his magazine ‘The Fra’ (Vol. 12, No. 6, p. 171, c. 1914) ↑ and catalogued in the “Misattributed” section of Wikiquote’s Marcus Aurelius page ↑. Its Stoic-sounding warmth is what pinned it, wrongly, to a Roman emperor.

source.heading: Where it really comes from

docMeta.dd: The Fra: A Journal of Affirmation, Vol. 12, No. 6 (c. 1914)

source.excerpt: When you arise in the morning, think of what a precious privilege it is to be alive — to breathe, to think, to enjoy, to love.
trail: Wikiquote’s Marcus Aurelius page ↑ lists this line under “Misattributed” and names the actual source as Elbert Hubbard’s magazine The Fra, Vol. 12, No. 6, p. 171.
The primary-source citation points to a scan I confirmed at Villanova’s Digital Library ↑, catalogued as “The Fra: a Journal of Affirmation, v.12 no.6” in the Hubbard Collection.
The line is absent from the sourced Meditations text on Wikiquote, yet is widely printed as Marcus Aurelius by aggregators such as Goodreads ↑, which cites Meditations with no locatable passage.
source.excerptNote: The wording popularly circulated as Marcus Aurelius. It is an Elbert Hubbard epigram; the em-dash is often rendered as a hyphen online.

sourceLink.text: The Fra, Vol. 12, No. 6 — Villanova Digital Library (Hubbard Collection)

source.rightsNote: The line first appeared in Elbert Hubbard’s magazine The Fra (Vol. 12, No. 6, c. 1914). A work published in the United States before 1931 is in the public domain, so this English original is free to reproduce. (The ancient Marcus Aurelius text to which it is falsely attributed is separately public-domain, but this wording is not his.)

author.name: Elbert Hubbard
author.heading: Who was Elbert Hubbard?
author.metaLine: 1856–1915 · American writer, publisher & founder of the Roycroft community
author.bio: Elbert Hubbard was an American writer, aphorist and publisher who founded the Roycroft arts-and-crafts community in East Aurora, New York, and edited the inspirational magazines The Philistine and The Fra. He is best known for the 1899 essay A Message to Garcia and for a torrent of pithy epigrams. Hubbard and his wife died in the sinking of the Lusitania in 1915.

misattribution.heading: How Hubbard became “Marcus Aurelius”
misattribution.intro: This is one of the internet’s most reproduced “Marcus Aurelius” lines — printed on mugs, posters, notebooks and meditation apps — yet it appears in none of his writing.

items.why: The sentence is in no translation of the Meditations; Wikiquote ↑ files it under “Misattributed” and identifies the real author as Elbert Hubbard in The Fra (Vol. 12, No. 6, p. 171).

Hubbard published the epigram in his own affirmation magazine, a scan of which survives in the Villanova Digital Library Hubbard Collection ↑. Hubbard’s upbeat aphorisms were frequently re-credited to more ancient or famous names.

misattribution.truthLine: The words are Elbert Hubbard’s, from The Fra around 1914 — later re-labelled as ancient Stoic wisdom and pinned on Marcus Aurelius ↑.

context.heading: Why the mix-up sticks
lead: Elbert Hubbard’s epigrams were engineered to be quotable: short, warm and self-improving. That same quality makes them easy to detach from their author and re-attach to whoever sounds more authoritative — and a morning meditation on being alive reads as effortlessly “Stoic.”

Marcus Aurelius is a magnet for feel-good attributions precisely because his real Meditations are private morning notes-to-self. A line about waking up grateful feels like him, so quote sites rarely stop to check that it isn’t in the text.
detailsBody: Search any full translation of the Meditations (Long, Farquharson, Hays, Hard) for “precious privilege” — it returns nothing.
Wikiquote lists the line in its Marcus Aurelius “Misattributed” section with a primary citation to Hubbard’s The Fra.
context.pull: It reads like Marcus Aurelius. It isn’t.
